It's tube strike time which again beckons the question - are we ready for driverless tubes?

Public support for ditching the 24-hour tube service wont be there, so that's the public and the government they're going against - it's not like previously where we could see a reason for rallying behind the closing of ticket offices (we'll forget the Bob Crow extra holiday/pay clause). This just seems like a union throwing its toys out of the chest and I think it's going to be one to their detriment.

The DLR does just fine and its front facing window gives a great view, it would be great to snake through London's caverns in the same way!

What do you guys think?
Can we just get on with driverless tubes?

It's hard to empathise with them this time. Also, something that I don't understand: won't 24h tube service mean --more-- jobs for drivers? Am I missing something? I don't really understand why they're protesting an increase in employment.

If the city started installing driverless trains there would, of course be strikes. Do you think that it'd be worth it in the long run? I wonder how much a two-day strike costs in terms of a hit to the city's productivity/economy etc. We have, what, two or three a tube strikes per year ? And if you go ahead installing driverless anyway. Maybe it's a net benefit to just accept the inevitable weeks of strikes. Just idly wondering. I don't really have a feeling for the figures.
It's not so much the economy that gets hit, more patience and the empathy of the London population!

They've hired 100-200 (can't remember the exact number) more tube drivers to cover the extra hours. Personally, I enjoy the strikes. They mean I get to work from home and get a lie in. But I also have difficulty seeing where the drivers are coming from this time given that the drivers have been offered pay rises and a £2000 one-off bonus, and they'll only be doing seven more night shifts a year than they are now.

If you haven't already seen CGPGrey's Humans Need Not Apply, watch it! It's a sobering exploration of the inevitability of automation, its overall benefit to society, and the imminent problems facing society as it loses jobs to automated systems. It asks more questions than it answers, and doesn't mention the Tube per se, but it does provide wider context to the issue.

While the it's easy to dismiss the Tube drivers as greedy whiners, it's going to be a bigger problem if they're all unemployed and homeless. (I can't imagine Tubing is a particularly transferable skill.)

Of course, I agree, it would leave a vacuum in their employment, but that to me gives more reason as to why they shouldn't suggest strikes! The worldwide use of driverless carriages should surely remind them that they are in fact replaceable. I know it's probably naive to say, but, nobody outside of the public sector gets to strike when they don't like their jobs, and since they're they ones primarily affected by the strikes, it makes it all that much harder to sympathise with.

I had posted a bunch of these over at /r/nfl_draft, but I figured I could start posting them here over the next few weeks.

QB, Michigan State, 6'4 220

Strengths:

  • Good arm, throws with zip on his passes and can make all the throws.

  • Goes progressions and makes his reads well, experience doing it in a pro style offense. Very good field vision.

  • Not a great athlete but can escape the pocket to extend plays. Comfortable throwing on the run and experienced with bootlegs.

  • Very accurate on short throws, when he misses it is almost always because of footwork.

Weaknesses:

  • Steps up into the pocket when there is outside pressure, but doesn't handle interior pressure well and can get jittery if it starts happening regularly.

  • Deep ball accuracy is a work in progress. In general good accuracy but footwork needs improvement.

  • Does not always step into his throws properly leading to some under thrown balls.

Overall: Right now Cook looks like the most polished quarterback prospect in the draft, but there are issues with him. His footwork isn't a huge worry but he must step into his throws or his passes with get jumped at the next level and get more comfortable stepping into interior pressure. Still, he looks the part of an NFL quarterback and is likely a top 10 pick next year.

Hello Sailors. I was wondering if any one here could give me advise on joining the Navy? I've posted in Reddit a few times but cant seem to get any responses.

I'm interested in becoming a Navy Corpsman. Knowing that the Navy supplies the medical support to the Marines, my first question is,

Q1: Do all Navy HM's have to serve with the Marines? Is there an option to opt out of that? Or are they just subject to the Navy's needs? I'm fairly physically fit, and If I absolutely had to, I know I could pass marine fitness standards. I really don't want to though. I'd rather just be a Corpsman for the Navy.

Q2: If there is not an option to opt out, from my understanding that would mean, at least at some point in my Navy career I would have to attend FMTB, correct?

Q3: I've done some more reading and from what I gather, at FMTB Sailors must pass several Navy PT tests, and must "Participate" in one Marine pt test. However it is not conditional to pass that marine pt test, for passing the school. Is that correct?

Q4: Let's say I was saddled with a Marine duty position. When they conduct their PFT tests, (I assume at least twice a year), do the Navy corpsman stationed with them have to meet Marine standards? Or are Navy fitness standards acceptable?

Thanks for any help you guys can give me. I'm interested in making a career out of the military. Please no unhelpful hateful comments. We all should have learned the golden rule as kids. If you haven't got something nice to say, hold your tongue. That's all I'm getting from reddit. Either no responses, or people calling me a faggot, pussy, weasel for not wanting to be a marine. You're right, I don't want to be a marine. It's just a little too Orrah! for me. I applaud you for your testicular fortitude, really I do. But I just want to be a Navy corpsman. And I don't think that is a bad thing to want to be. I'm not a strong runner. If I had to worry about making Marine pt standards twice a year I'd go fucking crazy. That's not how I want to spend the next 20 years.
HM who serve with Marines are called FMF. The majority of Navy Corpsman do not serve with Marines, they usually have shore duty in a base clinic or hospital.

There are many specialties and career paths within the HM rate as far as I understand. Not all of them serve with marines, but there is no "opt out". The military doesn't work like that. The most lucrative and highly trained position for a corpsman as far as I understand is becoming an independent duty corpsman. And you are required to adhere to Navy PRT standards, not the Marine standards. I am not an HM. But that is the best I could do to help you out. You should consider other rates as well, unless you are dead set on HM. What did you score on you'r ASVAB?
